stem: A café makes sandwiches from 4 kinds of bread and 5 fillings. Each sandwich has exactly one bread and one filling, and it comes either with exactly one of 3 sauces or with no sauce. How many different sandwiches are possible?
explanation: Choose the bread (4 ways), the filling (5 ways) and the sauce option. The sauce choice has 3 + 1 = 4 outcomes, because "no sauce" is a separate option. By the counting principle, 4 × 5 × 4 = 80. Forgetting the no-sauce option gives 4 × 5 × 3 = 60, and adding instead of multiplying gives 12.

stem: How many different arrangements of all five letters of the word CLIMB are there in which the letter I is neither the first letter nor the last letter?
explanation: Place I first: it can go only in one of the 3 middle positions. The other 4 letters then fill the remaining 4 positions in 4! = 24 ways, so there are 3 × 24 = 72 arrangements. Excluding only the first position gives 5! − 4! = 96, which still counts arrangements that end in I.

stem: A project team of 3 people is to be chosen from 7 engineers and 4 designers. How many different teams include exactly 1 designer?
explanation: Choose the designer in 4 ways and the 2 engineers in C(7, 2) = 21 ways; multiply to get 4 × 21 = 84. Adding the two counts (4 + 21 = 25) is the classic slip, and 130 = C(11, 3) − C(7, 3) counts teams with at least one designer, not exactly one.

stem: A fair six-sided die, with faces numbered 1 through 6, is rolled once, and a fair coin is tossed twice. What is the probability that the die shows a number greater than 4 and both tosses land heads? Give your answer as a fraction.
explanation: The die and the coins are independent, so multiply. P(die > 4) = 2/6 = 1/3, since only 5 and 6 qualify, and P(two heads) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The probability is 1/3 × 1/4 = 1/12. Counting 4 as "greater than 4" would give 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

stem: A bag contains 5 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random, one after the other, without replacement. What is the probability that both marbles are blue?
explanation: The first draw is blue with probability 3/8. After one blue marble is removed, 2 of the remaining 7 are blue, so the second draw is blue with probability 2/7. Multiply: 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28. Using 3/8 for both draws (9/64) treats the draws as if the marble were put back.

stem: A warehouse has three independent smoke alarms. In a fire, the alarms sound with probabilities 0.8, 0.7 and 0.5, respectively. What is the probability that at least one alarm sounds in a fire?
explanation: Use the complement: at least one sounds unless all three fail. The failure probabilities are 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5, so P(all fail) = 0.2 × 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.03 and P(at least one) = 1 − 0.03 = 0.97. The value 0.28 is the probability that all three sound, and 0.94 comes from leaving the third alarm out of the product.

stem: In a class of 40 students, 24 study French, 18 study Spanish and 7 study neither language. How many students study both French and Spanish?
explanation: Students who study at least one language number 40 − 7 = 33. By inclusion-exclusion, 24 + 18 − (both) = 33, so both = 42 − 33 = 9. Ignoring the 7 who study neither gives 24 + 18 − 40 = 2, which is the trap.

stem: A box contains n balls, exactly 3 of which are red. One ball is chosen at random. If the probability that the ball is red is at least 1/5 but less than 1/3, which of the following could be the value of n? Indicate all such values.
explanation: The probability is 3/n. From 3/n ≥ 1/5 we get n ≤ 15, and from 3/n < 1/3 we get n > 9, so n can be 10 through 15. That includes 10, 12 and 15. The value 9 gives exactly 1/3, which is not less than 1/3, and 16 gives 3/16, which is below 1/5.

stem: Of the 120 employees at a firm, 70 sometimes drive to work, 45 sometimes take the train, and 20 sometimes do both. How many of the employees never drive and never take the train?
explanation: Employees who use at least one of the two number 70 + 45 − 20 = 95, because the 20 who do both were counted twice. So 120 − 95 = 25 use neither. Forgetting to subtract the overlap gives 120 − 115 = 5.

stem: Six people, including Ana and Ben, are to sit in a row of six chairs. In how many different seating arrangements do Ana and Ben sit next to each other?
explanation: Treat Ana and Ben as one block: the block and the other 4 people can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Inside the block, Ana and Ben can sit in 2 orders, so the total is 2 × 120 = 240. Stopping at 120 forgets that Ben may sit on Ana's left or right.

stem: In a basketball league of 9 teams, each team plays every other team exactly twice, once at home and once away. How many games are played in all?
explanation: Each game is an ordered pair (home team, away team) of two different teams. There are 9 choices for the home team and 8 for the away team, so 9 × 8 = 72 games. Equivalently, C(9, 2) = 36 pairs of teams, each playing twice. Answering 36 counts each pair only once.

stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is neither 7 nor 11?
explanation: Of the 36 equally likely outcomes, 6 give a sum of 7 and 2 give a sum of 11 (5 + 6 and 6 + 5). So 36 − 8 = 28 outcomes qualify, and 28/36 = 7/9. Forgetting the 11 entirely gives 5/6; 2/9 is the probability of the excluded sums.

stem: How many three-digit positive integers have three different digits, all of which are odd?
explanation: There are 5 odd digits (1, 3, 5, 7, 9), and zero is not one of them, so the hundreds digit causes no extra restriction. Choose the digits in order: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. Allowing repeated digits gives 5³ = 125, and 10 = C(5, 3) ignores the order of the digits.

stem: Ten cards are numbered 1 through 10. Two cards are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers is even?
explanation: The sum is even when both cards are even or both are odd. P(both even) = 5/10 × 4/9 = 2/9, and P(both odd) is also 2/9, so the total is 4/9. The answer 1/2 would be right only with replacement; without replacement, a second card of the same parity is slightly less likely.

stem: For some positive integer n, the number of ways to choose 2 objects from a set of n different objects is x. Which of the following could be the value of x? Indicate all such values.
explanation: The number of ways is C(n, 2) = n(n − 1)/2, so x must be one of 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, ... (n = 5, 6, 7 and 8 give 10, 15, 21 and 28). The values 12, 18 and 24 fall between consecutive terms. A quick test is whether 2x is a product of two consecutive integers: 2 × 12 = 24 is not, but 2 × 21 = 42 = 7 × 6 is.

stem: How many different arrangements of the five letters of the word LEVEL are possible? (Arrangements that look identical count once.)
explanation: Five letters can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways if all are different. Here L appears twice and E appears twice, so divide by 2! for each repeated letter: 120/(2 × 2) = 30. Dividing by only one 2! gives 60, which still counts each arrangement twice.

stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled three times. What is the probability that at least one of the rolls shows a 6?
explanation: Use the complement. No 6 on a roll has probability 5/6, so no 6 in three rolls has probability (5/6)³ = 125/216, and at least one 6 has probability 1 − 125/216 = 91/216. Adding 1/6 three times gives 1/2, which double-counts outcomes with two or three 6s; 75/216 is the probability of exactly one 6.

stem: At a dinner for 50 guests, 30 guests ordered soup, 25 ordered salad and 12 ordered both. How many guests ordered exactly one of these two dishes?
explanation: Soup only is 30 − 12 = 18 and salad only is 25 − 12 = 13, so exactly one dish was ordered by 18 + 13 = 31 guests. (The remaining 50 − 31 − 12 = 7 ordered neither.) The tempting 43 = 30 + 25 − 12 counts guests who ordered at least one dish, which includes the 12 who had both.

stem: An integer is chosen at random from the integers 1 through 60, inclusive. What is the probability that the integer is divisible by 4 or by 6, or by both?
explanation: There are 15 multiples of 4 and 10 multiples of 6 from 1 to 60. Numbers divisible by both are the multiples of 12, and there are 5 of them, counted twice. So 15 + 10 − 5 = 20 integers qualify, and 20/60 = 1/3. Forgetting the overlap gives 25/60 = 5/12; using 24 as the overlap would miss that the least common multiple is 12.

stem: A club of 10 members, including Priya, will choose a president, a vice president and a treasurer, with no member holding more than one office. In how many ways can the three officers be chosen if Priya must be one of them?
explanation: Priya can take any of the 3 offices. The remaining two offices are then filled in order from the other 9 members in 9 × 8 = 72 ways. So there are 3 × 72 = 216 ways. Stopping at 72 assumes Priya's office is fixed, and 108 = 3 × C(9, 2) forgets that the other two offices are different from each other.

stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Which of the following events have a probability of exactly 1/6? Indicate all such events.
options: Both dice show the same number.
explanation: An event has probability 1/6 exactly when it contains 6 of the 36 outcomes. Doubles: 6 outcomes; a difference of 3: (1,4), (2,5), (3,6) and their reverses, 6 outcomes; a sum less than 5: sums of 2, 3 and 4 give 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 outcomes; a sum of 7: 6 outcomes. A sum of 8 has only 5 outcomes, and a product of 6 has only 4: (1,6), (6,1), (2,3), (3,2).

stem: A drawer contains 4 black socks and 6 white socks. If 2 socks are taken from the drawer at random, what is the probability that they are the same color?
explanation: There are C(10, 2) = 45 equally likely pairs. Matching pairs are C(4, 2) = 6 black pairs plus C(6, 2) = 15 white pairs, so the probability is 21/45 = 7/15. The answer 13/25 = 0.16 + 0.36 treats the second sock as if the first had been put back, and 8/15 is the probability of a mismatched pair.

stem: A parking permit code consists of 2 letters followed by 3 digits, such as KM 047. The 2 letters must be different, chosen from the 26 letters of the alphabet; the digits may be any of 0 through 9 and may repeat. How many different codes are possible?
explanation: Fill the positions in order: 26 choices for the first letter, 25 for the second (it must differ), and 10 for each digit. The count is 26 × 25 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 650,000. Allowing the letters to repeat would give 26² × 1,000 = 676,000, and using 10 × 9 × 8 for the digits wrongly forbids repeated digits.

stem: In a survey of 200 households, 120 own a cat or a dog or both. If 80 of the households own a dog and 30 own both a cat and a dog, how many households own a cat but not a dog?
explanation: Of the 120 households that own at least one of the pets, 80 own a dog, so the other 120 − 80 = 40 own a cat and no dog. Check: cat owners total 40 + 30 = 70, and 70 + 80 − 30 = 120. The trap 70 is the number of all cat owners, including the 30 that also own a dog; 50 is the number that own a dog but no cat.

stem: A reader will take 3 books on holiday, chosen from 5 different novels and 4 different poetry books. How many different selections include at least one poetry book?
explanation: Count all selections and subtract those with no poetry: C(9, 3) − C(5, 3) = 84 − 10 = 74. The tempting 4 × C(8, 2) = 112 first picks a poetry book and then any two others, so a selection with two poetry books is counted twice. The value 40 = 4 × C(5, 2) counts selections with exactly one poetry book.

stem: Mateo makes each free throw he attempts with probability 0.7, independently of his other attempts. If he attempts exactly two free throws, what is the probability that he makes exactly one of them?
explanation: Making the first and missing the second has probability 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.21, and missing the first and making the second also has probability 0.21. These are separate outcomes, so add: 0.21 + 0.21 = 0.42. The answer 0.21 counts only one of the two orders, and 0.91 is the probability of at least one success.

stem: An integer is chosen at random from the integers 1 through 30, inclusive. What is the probability that the integer has no prime factor in common with 30? Give your answer as a fraction.
explanation: Since 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, the integer must be divisible by none of 2, 3 and 5. These are 1, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29, so 8 of the 30 integers qualify, and 8/30 = 4/15. Do not forget 1, which has no prime factors at all, and do not count only the primes, which would include 2, 3 and 5 wrongly.

stem: Four different mathematics books and three different history books are to be placed in a row on a shelf. In how many arrangements are all four mathematics books next to one another?
explanation: Glue the four mathematics books into one block. The block and the 3 history books are 4 items, which can be ordered in 4! = 24 ways, and the books inside the block can be ordered in 4! = 24 ways, giving 24 × 24 = 576. Doubling to 1,152 for "either direction" counts again what the 4! inside the block already includes; 5,040 = 7! ignores the condition.

stem: Of the 80 students in a music school, 45 play in the orchestra and 38 sing in the choir. What is the least possible number of students who do both?
explanation: At most 80 students are in at least one group, and 45 + 38 = 83 exceeds 80 by 3, so at least 3 students must be counted in both. The value 3 is possible when every student is in at least one group. Answering 0 overlooks that the totals force an overlap, and 38 is the greatest possible overlap, not the least.

stem: Which of the following quantities are equal to 20? Indicate all such quantities.
options: The number of different arrangements of the letters A, A, B, B, B in a row
The number of ways to choose 3 people from a group of 6
The number of 2-person committees that can be formed from 7 people
The number of diagonals of a convex octagon
The number of ways to award a gold and a silver medal to 2 of 5 runners
explanation: C(6, 3) = 20; a convex octagon has C(8, 2) − 8 = 28 − 8 = 20 diagonals (pairs of vertices minus the 8 sides); and gold and silver can go to 5 × 4 = 20 ordered pairs of runners. The letters A, A, B, B, B have only 5!/(2! × 3!) = 10 arrangements, and C(7, 2) = 21, which is close to 20 but not equal.

stem: A quiz has 6 true-or-false questions. Olga guesses the answer to every question, and each guess is correct with probability 1/2, independently. What is the probability that she answers at least 5 questions correctly?
explanation: Each of the 2⁶ = 64 answer patterns is equally likely. Exactly 5 correct can happen in C(6, 5) = 6 ways (choose the one wrong answer), and all 6 correct in 1 way, so the probability is 7/64. The trap 3/32 = 6/64 counts only the patterns with exactly 5 correct and forgets the perfect score.

stem: Of 90 tourists on a trip, 52 visited the museum, 47 visited the gallery, and 15 visited neither. How many of the tourists visited exactly one of the two places?
explanation: First, 90 − 15 = 75 tourists visited at least one place. Then both = 52 + 47 − 75 = 24. Exactly one is the at-least-one group minus those who visited both: 75 − 24 = 51. The answer 24 is the overlap itself, and 28 = 52 − 24 counts only those who visited the museum alone.

stem: Kwame owns 7 different shirts and will pack 4 of them for a trip. If he will not pack both his blue shirt and his green shirt, how many different sets of 4 shirts can he pack?
explanation: Without the condition there are C(7, 4) = 35 sets. Sets that contain both the blue and the green shirt need 2 more shirts from the other 5: C(5, 2) = 10. So 35 − 10 = 25 sets are allowed. A common slip is to subtract the sets containing either shirt, but packing one of them alone is permitted.

stem: A jar holds 3 lemon, 4 cherry and 5 lime candies. Sofia takes 2 candies at random, one after the other, without replacement. What is the probability that at least one of the candies she takes is lime?
explanation: Find the complement, no lime: 7/12 for the first candy and 6/11 for the second, so P(no lime) = 42/132 = 7/22. Then P(at least one lime) = 1 − 7/22 = 15/22. The answer 95/144 = 1 − (7/12)² treats the draws as if the first candy were returned, and 35/66 is the probability of exactly one lime.

stem: Events A and B have P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. Which of the following could be the value of P(A or B), the probability that at least one of the events occurs? Indicate all such values.
explanation: P(A or B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − P(A and B). The overlap can be as large as 0.4 (B inside A), giving 0.5, and as small as 0 (A and B mutually exclusive), giving 0.9; every value in between is possible, including 0.7. P(A or B) can never be less than P(A) = 0.5, which rules out 0.2 and 0.4, and 1.0 would need a negative overlap.

stem: A robot moves along the lines of a square grid from the point (0, 0) to the point (4, 3). Each move takes it 1 unit to the right or 1 unit up. How many different paths can the robot take?
explanation: Every path has 7 moves: 4 to the right and 3 up. A path is determined by choosing which 3 of the 7 moves are up, so there are C(7, 3) = 35 paths. Multiplying 4 × 3 = 12 or adding 4 + 3 = 7 does not count the different orders of the moves.

stem: A shipment of 25 laptops contains exactly 5 defective laptops. An inspector chooses 2 laptops at random from the shipment. What is the probability that at least one of the 2 is defective?
explanation: P(neither defective) = 20/25 × 19/24 = 380/600 = 19/30, so P(at least one defective) = 1 − 19/30 = 11/30. The answer 9/25 = 1 − (4/5)² would apply only if the first laptop were put back before the second was chosen, and 1/3 is the probability of exactly one defective laptop.

stem: A spinner is divided into 5 equal sectors numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. The spinner is spun twice. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is even? Give your answer as a fraction.
explanation: A product is odd only when both numbers are odd. Three of the five numbers are odd, so P(odd product) = 3/5 × 3/5 = 9/25, and P(even product) = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25. Using 2/5 × 2/5 = 4/25 finds only the case where both numbers are even and misses the mixed cases.

stem: Five different gifts are to be given to 3 children. Each gift goes to exactly one child, and a child may receive any number of gifts, including none. In how many ways can the gifts be given?
explanation: Decide gift by gift: each of the 5 gifts can go to any of the 3 children, so there are 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 3⁵ = 243 ways. The trap 5³ = 125 reverses the roles, as if each child chose one of 5 gifts; 60 = 5 × 4 × 3 gives each child exactly one gift.

stem: In a city, 62 percent of adults read a morning news app, 47 percent read an evening news app, and 18 percent read neither. What percent of adults read both apps?
explanation: Adults who read at least one app make up 100 − 18 = 82 percent. Since 62 + 47 = 109 percent counts the overlap twice, both = 109 − 82 = 27 percent. The value 82 is the at-least-one group, and 29 = 47 − 18 subtracts the neither group from the wrong total.

stem: In a large group of adults, 60 percent are women. Of the women, 30 percent wear glasses, and of the men, 20 percent wear glasses. If an adult chosen at random from the group wears glasses, what is the probability that the adult is a woman?
explanation: Picture 100 adults: 60 women, of whom 18 wear glasses, and 40 men, of whom 8 wear glasses. Among the 26 who wear glasses, 18 are women, so the probability is 18/26 = 9/13. The answer 3/10 is the probability that a woman wears glasses, which reverses the condition, and 9/50 is the probability that a person is a woman who wears glasses.

stem: How many positive integers less than 1,000 have at least one digit equal to 7?
explanation: Count the complement. Write the integers 0 to 999 with three digits (007, 042, ...). Those with no digit 7 number 9 × 9 × 9 = 729, and this includes 000, so 728 positive integers below 1,000 have no 7. Hence 999 − 728 = 271 have at least one 7. Adding 100 + 100 + 100 = 300 (a 7 in each place) overcounts numbers such as 77 and 717.

stem: Each of the 100 students in a program takes at least one of three courses: art, biology and chemistry. Exactly 50 take art, 45 take biology, 40 take chemistry, and 10 take all three courses. How many students take exactly two of the three courses?
explanation: The course totals add to 50 + 45 + 40 = 135. A student in exactly one course is counted once, in exactly two courses twice, and in all three courses three times. So x + 2y + 3(10) = 135 and x + y + 10 = 100, giving x + 2y = 105 and x + y = 90, so y = 15. The trap 35 = 135 − 100 is the total number of extra counts, which includes two extra counts for each of the 10 students in all three courses.

stem: Six people, including Chen and Amara, sit at a round table with six identical chairs. Seatings that differ only by a rotation are considered the same. In how many different seatings are Chen and Amara not next to each other?
explanation: Around a round table, n people can be seated in (n − 1)! ways, so 6 people have 5! = 120 seatings. If Chen and Amara sit together, treat them as one unit: 5 units give 4! = 24 seatings, times 2 for their order, so 48. The answer is 120 − 48 = 72. The trap 48 is the number of seatings in which they are adjacent.

stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled n times. For which of the following values of n is the probability of rolling at least one 6 greater than 2/3? Indicate all such values.
explanation: P(at least one 6) = 1 − (5/6)ⁿ, so the condition is (5/6)ⁿ < 1/3. Now (5/6)⁶ = 15,625/46,656 ≈ 0.335, which is slightly more than 1/3, while (5/6)⁷ ≈ 0.279 is less. So n must be at least 7. The trap is to reason that 6 rolls give 6 × 1/6 = 1; adding the single-roll probabilities ignores overlap, and the true value for n = 6 is only about 0.665.

stem: Eight identical coins are to be shared among 3 children so that each child receives at least 1 coin. In how many different ways can this be done? (Only the number of coins each child gets matters.)
explanation: Line up the 8 coins; there are 7 gaps between neighbouring coins. Choosing 2 of the gaps as dividers splits the coins into three nonempty groups, so there are C(7, 2) = 21 ways. The trap 45 = C(10, 2) counts the shares in which a child may get no coins, and 56 = C(8, 3) chooses coins as if they were different.

stem: Three people are chosen at random, and each person's birth month is equally likely to be any of the 12 months, independently of the others. What is the probability that at least two of the three were born in the same month?
explanation: Find the probability that all three months differ: 12/12 × 11/12 × 10/12 = 1,320/1,728 = 55/72. The complement, at least two sharing a month, is 1 − 55/72 = 17/72. The tempting 1/4 adds 1/12 for each of the 3 pairs, which counts the case of all three sharing a month more than once; 55/72 is the probability of no match.

stem: A panel of 4 is to be chosen from 6 men and 5 women. How many different panels include at least 2 women?
explanation: Add the separate cases. Exactly 2 women: C(5, 2) × C(6, 2) = 10 × 15 = 150; exactly 3 women: C(5, 3) × 6 = 60; 4 women: C(5, 4) = 5. The total is 150 + 60 + 5 = 215. The trap 360 = C(5, 2) × C(9, 2) picks 2 women and then any 2 of the rest, which counts panels with 3 or 4 women several times; 150 stops at exactly 2 women.

stem: An integer is chosen at random from the three-digit integers 100 through 999. What is the probability that its digits are strictly increasing from left to right, as in 147?
explanation: Any 3 different nonzero digits can be written in increasing order in exactly one way, and 0 can never appear (it would have to come first). So there are C(9, 3) = 84 such integers out of 900, and 84/900 = 7/75. Including 0 gives C(10, 3) = 120 and 2/15, and 1/6 = 1/3! wrongly assumes every integer has three different digits.

stem: How many different arrangements of the six letters of the word BANANA are there in which the two letters N are not next to each other?
explanation: All arrangements: 6!/(3! × 2!) = 60, since A repeats 3 times and N twice. With the two N's together, treat NN as one tile: arrange B, A, A, A, NN in 5!/3! = 20 ways. So 60 − 20 = 40 arrangements keep the N's apart. The trap 20 is the number of arrangements in which the N's are adjacent.

stem: A coin is weighted so that it lands heads with probability 1/3 on each toss, independently. If the coin is tossed 4 times, what is the probability that it lands heads exactly twice? Give your answer as a fraction.
explanation: One particular order, such as HHTT, has probability (1/3)² × (2/3)² = 4/81. The 2 heads can occupy any 2 of the 4 tosses, which is C(4, 2) = 6 orders, so the probability is 6 × 4/81 = 24/81 = 8/27. Forgetting the factor 6 gives 4/81, and using 1/2 for each toss gives 3/8, which ignores the weighting.

stem: Of the 200 members of a music society, 140 like jazz and 120 like blues. At least 10 members like neither. If x members like both jazz and blues, what is the greatest possible value of x minus the least possible value of x?
explanation: At most 200 − 10 = 190 members like at least one style, so 140 + 120 − x ≤ 190 and x ≥ 70. The overlap cannot exceed the smaller group, so x ≤ 120 (every blues fan also likes jazz, leaving 60 who like neither, which satisfies the condition). The difference is 120 − 70 = 50. Answering 70 gives only the least value, and 60 uses 200 instead of 190 for the least value.

stem: Four married couples attend a workshop. Two of the eight people are chosen at random to give a presentation together. What is the probability that the two chosen are married to each other?
explanation: There are C(8, 2) = 28 equally likely pairs, and 4 of them are couples, so the probability is 4/28 = 1/7. Another way: whoever is chosen first, exactly 1 of the 7 remaining people is that person's spouse. The trap 1/8 divides by 8 people instead of the 7 people left after the first choice.

stem: Three boys and three girls are to stand in a row for a photograph so that no two boys stand next to each other and no two girls stand next to each other. How many such arrangements are possible?
explanation: The pattern must alternate, either BGBGBG or GBGBGB, so there are 2 patterns. In each pattern the boys can fill their places in 3! = 6 ways and the girls in 3! = 6 ways, giving 2 × 6 × 6 = 72. The answer 36 forgets that the row may start with a girl, and 144 counts each arrangement twice.

stem: From a set of 10 different objects, k objects are to be chosen, where order does not matter. For which of the following values of k is the number of possible choices greater than 100? Indicate all such values.
explanation: The counts are C(10, 2) = 45, C(10, 3) = 120, C(10, 4) = 210 and C(10, 5) = 252. Choosing k objects is the same as leaving out 10 − k, so C(10, 7) = C(10, 3) = 120 and C(10, 8) = C(10, 2) = 45. Thus k = 3, 4, 5 and 7 work. The trap is to think the counts keep growing with k; they peak at k = 5 and then fall.

stem: Two different integers are chosen at random from the integers 1 through 9, inclusive. What is the probability that their product is even?
explanation: The product is odd only if both integers are odd. There are 5 odd integers, so C(5, 2) = 10 of the C(9, 2) = 36 pairs are both odd, and P(even) = 1 − 10/36 = 26/36 = 13/18. The trap 56/81 = 1 − (5/9)² treats the two choices as if the same integer could be chosen twice, and 5/18 is the probability of an odd product.

stem: Of the 60 students in a class, 35 belong to the drama club and 28 belong to the debate club. Which of the following could be the number of students who belong to neither club? Indicate all such numbers.
explanation: If b students belong to both clubs, then 63 − b belong to at least one, and neither = 60 − (63 − b) = b − 3. The overlap b must be at least 3 (so that at most 60 students are in a club) and at most 28 (the smaller club), so neither ranges from 0 to 25, taking every whole number in between. The values 28 and 32 would need an overlap larger than the debate club itself.

stem: A bag contains r red tiles and 5 blue tiles. Two tiles are drawn at random without replacement. For which of the following values of r is the probability that both tiles are red greater than 1/3? Indicate all such values.
explanation: P(both red) = r(r − 1)/[(r + 5)(r + 4)]. For r = 7 this is 42/132 ≈ 0.318, just below 1/3, and for r = 8 it is 56/156 ≈ 0.359, above 1/3. Since the probability rises as r grows, r = 8, 9 and 10 work (9 gives 72/182 ≈ 0.396 and 10 gives 90/210 ≈ 0.429). With replacement, r = 7 would give (7/12)² ≈ 0.340 and would wrongly be included.

stem: How many four-digit positive integers are even and have four different digits?
explanation: Split by the units digit. If it is 0, the other places have 9 × 8 × 7 = 504 choices. If it is 2, 4, 6 or 8 (4 ways), the thousands digit cannot be 0 or the units digit, leaving 8 choices, then 8 and 7 for the middle places: 4 × 8 × 8 × 7 = 1,792. The total is 504 + 1,792 = 2,296. The trap 2,520 = 5 × 9 × 8 × 7 ignores that 0 can be the units digit but not the thousands digit.

stem: Ravi and Lena each choose 2 of the same 6 different books at random, independently of each other. What is the probability that they choose at least one book in common?
explanation: Whatever pair Ravi picks, Lena picks one of C(6, 2) = 15 pairs. She avoids both of Ravi's books only by choosing 2 of the other 4 books, in C(4, 2) = 6 ways, so P(no book in common) = 6/15 = 2/5 and P(at least one) = 1 − 2/5 = 3/5. The trap 8/15 counts only the pairs with exactly one shared book and forgets the 1 pair identical to Ravi's.

qa: The number of ways to arrange 4 different books in a row on a shelf
qb: The number of ways to choose 4 books from 5 different books
explanation: Arranging 4 books in a row: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 ways. Choosing 4 of 5 books, where order does not matter, is the same as choosing the 1 book to leave out: 5 ways. So Quantity A is greater. Do not confuse arrangements (order matters) with selections (order does not).

qa: The number of ways to choose 3 people from a group of 9
qb: The number of ways to choose 6 people from a group of 9
explanation: Every choice of 3 people to include matches exactly one choice of 6 people to leave behind, so the counts are equal: C(9, 3) = C(9, 6) = 84. A hurried reader may assume that choosing more people gives more possibilities, but the counts are symmetric about half of the group.

stem: A fair coin is tossed 3 times.
qa: The probability of getting exactly 2 heads
qb: The probability of getting at least 2 heads
explanation: Of the 8 equally likely outcomes, 3 have exactly 2 heads (HHT, HTH, THH), so Quantity A is 3/8. At least 2 heads also includes HHH, so Quantity B is 4/8 = 1/2. Quantity B is greater, because "at least 2" contains every outcome counted in "exactly 2" and one more.

stem: In a group of 30 people, 18 have a passport and 15 have a driving licence.
qa: The number of people who have both a passport and a driving licence
explanation: Since 18 + 15 = 33 is 3 more than 30, at least 3 people must have both, so the overlap is at least 3. It could be exactly 3 (if everyone has at least one document) or as large as 15 (if every licence holder also has a passport). Quantity A could equal 3 or be greater, so the relationship cannot be determined. Stopping at the minimum makes the quantities look equal.

stem: Two cards are drawn at random, without replacement, from five cards numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.
qa: The probability that the sum of the two numbers is odd
explanation: The sum is odd when one card is odd and the other even. There are 3 odd and 2 even cards, so P(odd sum) = 3/5 × 2/4 + 2/5 × 3/4 = 6/20 + 6/20 = 3/5, which is greater than 1/2. Thinking "odd and even are equally likely" gives 1/2 and the wrong answer; the cards are not balanced between odd and even.

stem: n is a positive integer.
qa: The number of ways to arrange n different objects in a row
explanation: Quantity A is n!. For n = 1, 2 and 3, n! is 1, 2 and 6, while 2ⁿ is 2, 4 and 8, so B is greater. For n = 4, 4! = 24 is greater than 2⁴ = 16, and n! stays ahead after that. Because the comparison changes with n, it cannot be determined. Testing only small values suggests B is always greater.

stem: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.5.
qa: The probability that exactly one of the events A and B occurs
qb: The probability that either both events occur or neither occurs
explanation: Exactly one: 0.6 × 0.5 + 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.30 + 0.20 = 0.5. Both or neither: 0.6 × 0.5 + 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.30 + 0.20 = 0.5. The two quantities are equal, and they must add to 1 because together they cover every outcome. Here P(B) = 0.5 makes them equal whatever P(A) is; it is tempting to guess that "both or neither" is smaller because "both" sounds unlikely.

qa: The number of 3-letter strings that can be formed from the letters A, B, C and D if letters may repeat
qb: The number of 3-letter strings that can be formed from the letters A, B, C, D, E and F if no letter may repeat
explanation: Quantity A: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. Quantity B: 6 × 5 × 4 = 120. Quantity B is greater. Allowing repetition increases the count for a fixed set of letters, but here B has more letters to choose from, which matters more.

stem: k is an integer and 0 ≤ k ≤ 8.
qa: The number of ways to choose k objects from 8 different objects
explanation: The values of C(8, k) for k = 0 to 8 are 1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1. The largest is C(8, 4) = 70, so Quantity A is either less than 70 or equal to it. Since both relationships are possible, the answer is that it cannot be determined. Seeing that A can never exceed 70 tempts many to pick B, but k = 4 makes the quantities equal.

stem: A bag contains 4 red balls and 6 green balls. One ball is chosen at random.
qa: The probability that the ball is red
explanation: The probability of red is 4 red balls out of 10, or 0.4, which is less than 0.6. The value 0.6 is the probability of green. A common slip is to compare the ratio of red to green, 4/6 ≈ 0.67, instead of red to the total.

stem: A set menu offers 3 starters, 4 main courses and 2 desserts. A diner chooses exactly one of each. How many different meals are possible?
explanation: Each starter can be paired with each main course and each dessert, so multiply: 3 × 4 × 2 = 24. Adding 3 + 4 + 2 = 9 counts single dishes, not complete meals.

stem: One letter is chosen at random from the seven letters of the word PROBLEM. What is the probability that the letter is a vowel?
explanation: PROBLEM has 7 letters, and 2 of them, O and E, are vowels, so the probability is 2/7. The answer 2/5 compares vowels with consonants (2 to 5) instead of vowels with all letters, and 5/7 is the probability of a consonant.

stem: Seven colleagues meet, and each person shakes hands exactly once with each of the others. How many handshakes take place?
explanation: A handshake is a pair of people, so count pairs: C(7, 2) = (7 × 6)/2 = 21. The product 7 × 6 = 42 counts each handshake twice, once from each person's side.

stem: Each of 25 people at a meeting likes tea or coffee or both. If 15 like tea and 13 like coffee, how many like both?
explanation: Everyone is in at least one group, so 15 + 13 − (both) = 25, and both = 28 − 25 = 3. The value 28 is the sum of the two groups before the overlap is removed, and 12 = 15 − 3 is the number who like only tea.

stem: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability that both land tails?
explanation: The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT, and only TT has two tails, so the probability is 1/4. The trap 1/3 lists only "two heads, one of each, two tails", but "one of each" happens in two ways and is twice as likely as the others.

stem: A coach must choose a starting team of 5 players from a squad of 9, and the team captain must be one of the 5. How many different starting teams are possible?
explanation: The captain's place is fixed, so choose the other 4 players from the remaining 8: C(8, 4) = 70. The trap 126 = C(9, 5) ignores the condition, and 56 = C(8, 5) wrongly picks 5 more players in addition to the captain.

stem: How many different arrangements of the five letters of the word PAPER are possible?
explanation: If all five letters were different there would be 5! = 120 arrangements. The two P's are identical, so each arrangement is counted twice, and there are 120/2 = 60. The trap 30 divides by an extra 2 as if a second letter repeated, but only P appears twice.

stem: An integer is chosen at random from the integers 1 through 20, inclusive. Which of the following events have a probability greater than 1/4? Indicate all such events.
options: The integer is a multiple of 3.
The integer is a multiple of 4.
The integer is a perfect square.
explanation: An event needs more than 5 of the 20 integers. Primes: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, which is 8; multiples of 3: 6; even integers: 10. Multiples of 4 number exactly 5, giving exactly 1/4, which is not greater than 1/4, and perfect squares (1, 4, 9, 16) number only 4.

stem: In a class of 12 students, 4 are left-handed. Two students are chosen at random. What is the probability that both are left-handed? Give your answer as a fraction.
explanation: There are C(12, 2) = 66 possible pairs and C(4, 2) = 6 left-handed pairs, so the probability is 6/66 = 1/11. Equivalently, 4/12 × 3/11 = 1/11. Using 4/12 × 4/12 = 1/9 forgets that the first student chosen is no longer available.

stem: A 4-character code is made from the letters A, B, C, D and E, and letters may repeat. How many codes contain the letter A at least once?
explanation: There are 5⁴ = 625 codes in all, and 4⁴ = 256 of them use only B, C, D and E. So 625 − 256 = 369 codes contain at least one A. The trap 256 is the number of codes with no A, not the number with an A.

stem: Three fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that all three show different numbers?
explanation: The first die can show anything, the second must differ from it (5/6), and the third must differ from both (4/6). So P = 5/6 × 4/6 = 20/36 = 5/9. The trap 35/36 is 1 minus the probability that all three match, but "not all the same" still allows two dice to match.

stem: How many subsets of the set {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} contain at least one even number? (Count the empty set as a subset.)
explanation: A set of 6 elements has 2⁶ = 64 subsets. The subsets with no even number are the subsets of {1, 3, 5}, and there are 2³ = 8 of them, including the empty set. So 64 − 8 = 56 subsets contain an even number. Subtracting 7 instead of 8 forgets that the empty set also has no even number.

stem: From a group of 5 people, a committee of k people is formed, and one of its members is named chair. For which of the following values of k is the number of different possible committees with a chair greater than 25? Indicate all such values.
explanation: Choose the k members in C(5, k) ways and then the chair in k ways, giving k × C(5, k). The values are 5, 20, 30, 20 and 5 for k = 1 to 5, so only k = 3 gives more than 25. It is tempting to include k = 4 or 5 because larger committees seem to allow more choices, but C(5, 4) and C(5, 5) are small.

stem: In a family with 4 children, each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl, independently of the others. If at least one of the children is a girl, what is the probability that at least two are girls?
explanation: Of the 16 equally likely families, 15 have at least one girl, which is the new sample space. Families with at least two girls number 16 − 1 − 4 = 11 (removing the all-boy family and the 4 with exactly one girl). So the probability is 11/15. The trap 11/16 ignores the given condition and divides by all 16 families.

stem: In a club of 50 members, 28 play chess, 21 play go, and 9 play both games. If a member is chosen at random, what is the probability that the member plays exactly one of the two games?
explanation: Chess only: 28 − 9 = 19. Go only: 21 − 9 = 12. So 19 + 12 = 31 members play exactly one game, and the probability is 31/50. The trap 4/5 = 40/50 counts members who play at least one game, which includes the 9 who play both.
